title: Dog Brains Can Tell Angry Faces From Fearful Ones
summary:
Dogs already seem to know when a leash or a jingling key means a walk. A new study suggests they can also tell some human emotions apart just by looking at faces.

Laura Cuaya, a neuroscientist at the University of Vienna in Austria, and her team trained 14 family dogs to lie still inside an MRI scanner that measures brain activity. The dogs included border collies and golden retrievers. Cuaya said the animals were very good at the task.

In one test, dogs saw photos of unfamiliar people looking happy or neutral. Happy faces lit up a reward-related brain area more than neutral faces. In another test, the dogs saw faces showing different negative feelings. Their brains responded differently to angry or sad faces than to fearful ones.

The researchers reported the results August 10 in the journal iScience. Cuaya says this is the first evidence that dogs can distinguish among negative emotions on human faces, not only “good” versus “bad.” Earlier work had already shown positive and negative expressions activate different brain regions.

Cuaya cautions that the findings may not apply to every breed, because this study focused on border collies and golden retrievers. Her group is also studying how dog brains react to a sound thought to be like dog laughter. They are not planning similar MRI work with cats, which are harder to keep still in a scanner.

The research offers another reason to smile at a pup you meet—they might read more of your face than you think.
why_it_matters: Understanding how dogs read faces can deepen respect for pets as emotional partners. It also shows how careful brain science tests ideas about animal minds.
